--- title: "Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend" description: "Compare all four distance grid backends (rust_exact, rust_aabb, rust_aabb_interp, cpu/dask), pick the right one for your system size, and learn which two methods to never use." image: tutorial_images/distance_grid_isosurface.png jupyter: python3 execute: freeze: true --- ## Overview The distance grid is the foundation of every `mofography` pore analysis — segmentation, RAG, PSD, PLD, and surface area all consume the same `dgrid` array. **Which function you call to build that array matters** because each backend trades off accuracy, memory, and runtime differently, and two of the legacy backends are *unsafe* on non-orthogonal cells. This tutorial covers: 1. The four **active** distance grid backends and their exact signatures 2. A **decision tree** mapping system size to the right method 3. The **auto-AABB** policy the interactive app uses 4. ⚠️ The two **broken** methods to *never* use and why If you have not done so, please complete the [Distance Grid tutorial](distance_grid.qmd) first — the rest of this page assumes you understand what a `dgrid` is and what `spacing` controls. ## The four distance grid backends | # | Function | Strategy | Best for | Status | |---|----------|----------|----------|--------| | 1 | `dgrid_from_atoms_rust` | Brute-force Rust, exact MIC, thread-parallel | **All systems — default** | ✅ Active | | 2 | `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust` | R-tree (AABB) neighbor search in Rust | Large systems, memory-constrained | ✅ Active | | 3 | `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust` | Coarse AABB + trilinear interpolation | Very large systems, mild smoothing OK | ✅ Active | | 4 | `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu` | freud `AABBQuery` + Dask, Python | Legacy compatibility | ⚠️ Legacy | ::: {.callout-warning} ## ⚠️ Do NOT use these two methods **`dgrid_from_atoms_gpu`** and **`dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb`** are **BROKEN on non-orthogonal (skewed) cells**. They compute the minimum-image convention with per-axis `NINT`, which is *only* correct for orthogonal cells. Most MOFs (and all triclinic/monoclinic cells) violate this assumption, so these functions produce *systematically wrong* distance grids on real materials. They are kept in the codebase for legacy code paths but **must not be used in new work**. The Rust backend uses the same correct MIC path for every cell type. See the [Broken methods](#broken-methods) section for details. ::: ## Signatures ### 1. `dgrid_from_atoms_rust` — exact, brute-force ```python dgrid_from_atoms_rust(ase_atoms, spacing, radii=None) ``` | Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning | |-----------|------|---------|---------| | `ase_atoms` | `ase.Atoms` | — | Framework structure | | `spacing` | `float` | — | Grid spacing in Å | | `radii` | `np.ndarray` or `None` | `None` | Per-atom VDW radii (Å). `None` → Bondi (1964) with Mendeleev fill | **Returns:** `np.ndarray` of shape `(nx, ny, nz)`, signed distance to the nearest atom surface. **Strategy:** Thread-parallel (Rayon) brute-force — every grid point is checked against every atom using an *exact* minimum-image convention. Orthogonal cells use a SIMD-optimized SoA path; skewed cells fall back to a 7-image Wassenaar construction. O(N_atoms × N_grid) work, O(N_grid) memory. **Use when:** you want the most accurate distance grid and you have enough RAM for one float32 per voxel. ### 2. `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust` — R-tree, memory-efficient ```python dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(ase_atoms, spacing, radii=None, n_neighbors=10) ``` | Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning | |-----------|------|---------|---------| | `ase_atoms` | `ase.Atoms` | — | Framework structure | | `spacing` | `float` | — | Grid spacing in Å | | `radii` | `np.ndarray` or `None` | `None` | Per-atom VDW radii (Å) | | `n_neighbors` | `int` | `10` | Number of nearest atoms to query per grid point | **Strategy:** Builds a Rust AABB (axis-aligned bounding box) tree on the atoms, then queries `n_neighbors` nearest atoms for every grid point under PBC. The minimum of `dist - radii[nbr]` becomes the surface distance. Memory is dominated by the R-tree, *not* by the grid → much smaller RAM footprint than brute force on large cells. **Use when:** cells > 50 Å or atoms > 1000 and the brute-force Rust path runs out of memory. Accuracy depends on `n_neighbors`: 10 is safe for typical MOFs; reduce to 4–6 if the structure has very large open channels where the nearest atoms may be far apart, and consider whether you need 20+ for tiny-pore systems. ### 3. `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust` — coarse + trilinear ```python dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust( ase_atoms, spacing, coarse_factor=2, radii=None, n_neighbors=10, ) ``` | Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning | |-----------|------|---------|---------| | `ase_atoms` | `ase.Atoms` | — | Framework structure | | `spacing` | `float` | — | **Fine** grid spacing in Å | | `coarse_factor` | `int` | `2` | Coarsening factor for the AABB sampling grid (must be > 1) | | `radii` | `np.ndarray` or `None` | `None` | Per-atom VDW radii (Å) | | `n_neighbors` | `int` | `10` | AABB neighbor count | **Returns:** `np.ndarray` (float32) of shape `(nx, ny, nz)` matching the *fine* `spacing`. **Strategy:** Computes the AABB distance grid on a **coarse** grid (spacing × `coarse_factor`), then trilinearly interpolates back to the fine grid. Reduces compute by `coarse_factor³` (default 8×) and *also* acts as a mild low-pass filter. The grid shape is identical to the brute-force result, so downstream code is unchanged. **Use when:** systems so large that even the AABB Rust path is too slow, *and* you can tolerate a slightly smoother distance field (mild trilinear averaging of nearby values). Good for HT screens where you want a ballpark PSD, less ideal for resolving sub-Å features like pore-limiting windows. Increase `coarse_factor` to 3 or 4 for very large cells; decrease toward 1 (in practice, use the plain AABB method) when you need sharper windows. ### 4. `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu` — freud + Dask, Python ```python dgrid_from_atoms_cpu( ase_atoms, radii=None, spacing=0.25, block_size=50000, n_neighbors=10, probe_radius=0, precompute=True, ) ``` | Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning | |-----------|------|---------|---------| | `ase_atoms` | `ase.Atoms` | — | Framework structure | | `radii` | `np.ndarray` or `None` | `None` | Per-atom VDW radii (Å). `None` → uses a hand-rolled Bondi table | | `spacing` | `float` | `0.25` | Grid spacing in Å | | `block_size` | `int` | `50000` | Dask chunk size (grid points per block) | | `n_neighbors` | `int` | `10` | AABB neighbor count for freud query | | `probe_radius` | `float` | `0` | Probe radius added on top of atom radii (Å) | | `precompute` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, call `.compute()` and return a NumPy array; if `False`, return a lazy Dask array | **Strategy:** Builds a freud `AABBQuery` on the framework, lays out the grid as a Dask array of `block_size` chunks, and maps `gpd_aabb` (a NumPy reduction over the freud neighbor list) over every block. Uses `complete_cell().T` for the box, so the **MIC is correct on skewed cells** — this is *not* one of the broken methods. **Use when:** you need Python-level introspection of intermediate values, are running on a machine without the Rust extension, or want lazy Dask composition with other grid ops. Performance is generally 5–20× slower than the Rust path on the same machine. ## Decision tree ```mermaid flowchart TD A[System: ASE Atoms + spacing] --> B{Atoms × grid voxels
fits in RAM
and runtime OK?} B -- Yes --> C[rust_exact
dgrid_from_atoms_rust] B -- No, OOM or too slow --> D{Is mild smoothing
of the dgrid OK?} D -- Yes --> E[rust_aabb_interp
dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust] D -- No, need exact --> F[rust_aabb
dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust] A --> G[Need Python-level
introspection?] G -- Yes --> H[cpu / Dask
dgrid_from_atoms_cpu] G -- No --> C A -.->|NEVER| X[gpu or cpu_no_aabb
broken on skewed cells] X -.->|redirect| C ``` ### Rule of thumb | System size (atoms × grid voxels) | Recommended method | Why | |------------------------------------|--------------------|-----| | < 5 × 10⁷ (small-to-medium) | `dgrid_from_atoms_rust` | Brute-force is fast enough and the most accurate | | 5 × 10⁷ to 5 × 10⁸ (large) | `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust` | AABB tree cuts memory; same accuracy as brute force | | > 5 × 10⁸ (very large, HT screens) | `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust` with `coarse_factor=2` or `3` | 8–27× compute savings; smooths fine features | | Need Python / Dask composition | `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu` | Slowest but flexible; uses correct freud MIC | These are rough numbers — the actual crossover depends on cell shape, number of periodic images the AABB has to handle, and how much RAM you have. The auto-AABB policy in the interactive app uses a similar memory budget to switch. ## Auto-AABB policy (interactive app) The Streamlit app (`mofography_dash` / hosted demo) does **not** expose the distance-grid method as a user knob by default. Instead it runs a two-step policy: 1. **Estimate** the float32 memory cost of the brute-force grid: `4 × nx × ny × nz` bytes. 2. **If** that estimate exceeds the configured RAM budget (default: ~512 MB), it auto-switches to `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust` with `n_neighbors=10` (or to `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust` with `coarse_factor=2` for very large systems). A short status line in the UI tells you which backend was used. This means the app "just works" for both IRMOF-1 and a 100-atom × 200-Å supercell, but it also means you should *check the UI output* before running a 1000-frame batch — silently hitting the AABB path on a system that needs brute-force precision can change window diameters by a few percent. The notebook and CLI surfaces do **not** auto-switch; you choose the backend explicitly. ## Setup ::: {#26a0ee33 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import mofography as mgr from ase.io import read import numpy as np import time # Load a MOF structure atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif") # 424 atoms, ~26 Å cubic cell print(f"Loaded {len(atoms)} atoms, cell: {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Loaded 424 atoms, cell: [25.83 25.83 25.83] ``` ::: ::: ## Method 1: `dgrid_from_atoms_rust` (default) ::: {#1fdabd93 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} t0 = time.perf_counter() dgrid_exact = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5) t_exact = time.perf_counter() - t0 print(f"rust_exact: shape={dgrid_exact.shape}, " f"min={dgrid_exact.min():.2f}, max={dgrid_exact.max():.2f}, " f"time={t_exact*1000:.0f} ms") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rust_exact: shape=(52, 52, 52), min=-1.70, max=7.54, time=48 ms ``` ::: ::: **Pros:** exact MIC for all cell types, thread-parallel, no accuracy trade-off. **Cons:** O(N_atoms × N_grid) — memory scales with grid size. ## Method 2: `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust` (memory-efficient) ::: {#caa6e1df .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} t0 = time.perf_counter() dgrid_aabb = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, n_neighbors=10) t_aabb = time.perf_counter() - t0 print(f"rust_aabb: shape={dgrid_aabb.shape}, " f"min={dgrid_aabb.min():.2f}, max={dgrid_aabb.max():.2f}, " f"time={t_aabb*1000:.0f} ms") # Agreement with exact method print(f"max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_aabb| = {np.abs(dgrid_exact - dgrid_aabb).max():.3e}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rust_aabb: shape=(52, 52, 52), min=-1.70, max=7.54, time=36 ms max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_aabb| = 0.000e+00 ``` ::: ::: Uses a Rust AABB tree to find nearby atoms for each grid point. `n_neighbors` controls the search radius — higher = more accurate but slower. For typical MOFs, `n_neighbors=10` agrees with the exact method to ~1e-3 Å. If you see a few-voxel disagreement near a wall, raise `n_neighbors` to 16 or 20. ## Method 3: `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust` (very large systems) ::: {#0c6a3d9f .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} t0 = time.perf_counter() dgrid_interp = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust( atoms, spacing=0.5, coarse_factor=2, n_neighbors=10, ) t_interp = time.perf_counter() - t0 print(f"rust_aabb+int: shape={dgrid_interp.shape}, " f"min={dgrid_interp.min():.2f}, max={dgrid_interp.max():.2f}, " f"time={t_interp*1000:.0f} ms") print(f"max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_interp| = {np.abs(dgrid_exact - dgrid_interp).max():.3e}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rust_aabb+int: shape=(52, 52, 52), min=-1.26, max=7.54, time=8 ms max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_interp| = 8.061e-01 ``` ::: ::: The coarse grid is at 1.0 Å spacing (spacing × coarse_factor), and the result is trilinearly interpolated back to 0.5 Å. The interpolation step is what introduces the mild smoothing — you can see it as a slight rounding of the surface near tight windows. **Do not** crank `coarse_factor` above ~3 if you care about sub-Å window diameters; beyond that the interpolation swamps the true signal. ## Method 4: `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu` (legacy / Python) ::: {#5b855c78 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} t0 = time.perf_counter() dgrid_cpu = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000) t_cpu = time.perf_counter() - t0 print(f"cpu/dask: shape={dgrid_cpu.shape}, " f"min={dgrid_cpu.min():.2f}, max={dgrid_cpu.max():.2f}, " f"time={t_cpu*1000:.0f} ms") # Note: dgrid_from_atoms_cpu is correct on skewed cells (uses freud AABB) print(f"max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_cpu| = {np.abs(dgrid_exact - dgrid_cpu).max():.3e}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` cpu/dask: shape=(52, 52, 52), min=-1.98, max=7.54, time=1033 ms max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_cpu| = 2.800e-01 ``` ::: ::: 5–20× slower than the Rust path on a single thread, but the Dask graph is composable: pass `precompute=False` to get a lazy array and chain downstream reductions. This is the right entry point if you need to plug `dgrid` into an existing Dask pipeline. ## Side-by-side timing ::: {#edb7c572 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} methods = { "rust_exact": mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5), "rust_aabb": mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, n_neighbors=10), "rust_aabb+int": mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, coarse_factor=2), "cpu/dask": mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000), } ref = methods["rust_exact"] print(f"{'method':<18} {'shape':<14} {'min':>7} {'max':>7} max|diff|") for name, g in methods.items(): diff = float(np.abs(g - ref).max()) if name != "rust_exact" else 0.0 print(f"{name:<18} {str(g.shape):<14} {g.min():>7.2f} {g.max():>7.2f} {diff:.3e}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` method shape min max max|diff| rust_exact (52, 52, 52) -1.70 7.54 0.000e+00 rust_aabb (52, 52, 52) -1.70 7.54 0.000e+00 rust_aabb+int (52, 52, 52) -1.26 7.54 8.061e-01 cpu/dask (52, 52, 52) -1.98 7.54 2.800e-01 ``` ::: ::: ## Broken methods ::: {.callout-danger} ## Two functions you must NOT use: `dgrid_from_atoms_gpu` and `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb` Both compute the **minimum-image convention** with per-axis `NINT` rounding: ```python # WRONG on a skewed cell dx = dx - cell[0, 0] * NINT(dx / cell[0, 0]) dy = dy - cell[1, 1] * NINT(dy / cell[1, 1]) dz = dz - cell[2, 2] * NINT(dz / cell[2, 2]) ``` This is **only correct for orthogonal cells** (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic). On a monoclinic or triclinic cell — which includes most real MOFs — the per-axis NINT picks the wrong image for some atom–grid pairs, and the distance grid develops systematic stripes near the cell walls. The bug is silent: the function returns without warning and the dgrid *looks* plausible until you compare it to the exact result. **Use the Rust backend (`dgrid_from_atoms_rust`) instead.** Its MIC path uses a 7-image Wassenaar construction on skewed cells, which is correct for all cell types. The CPU/Dask method (`dgrid_from_atoms_cpu`, *without* the `_no_aabb` suffix) is also correct because it routes through freud's AABB query, which uses the proper box geometry. If you see `dgrid_from_atoms_gpu` or `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb` in legacy code, replace the call with: ```python # Replace dgrid_from_atoms_gpu(...) dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5) # Replace dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb(...) dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000) ``` ::: ## Parameter guide | Parameter | Applies to | Default | Typical range | What it controls | |-----------|------------|---------|---------------|------------------| | `spacing` | all | — | 0.2 – 1.0 Å | Voxel edge length. Halving → 8× voxels. | | `radii` | all | `None` | — | Override per-atom VDW radii (Å). `None` → Bondi (1964) + Mendeleev fill. | | `n_neighbors` | AABB, interp, CPU | `10` | 4 – 20 | Number of nearest atoms queried per voxel. | | `coarse_factor` | interp | `2` | 2 – 4 | Coarsening of the sampling grid. | | `block_size` | CPU | `50000` | 10k – 200k | Dask chunk size (grid points per block). | | `precompute` | CPU | `True` | bool | `True` → return NumPy; `False` → return lazy Dask array. | | `probe_radius` | CPU | `0` | 0 – 5 Å | Extra probe radius added on top of `radii`. | **Tip:** Start with `dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5)` and only switch to AABB or interp when you hit a memory or runtime wall. ## Quick decision recap - **Default → `dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5)`** — exact MIC, correct for all cell types. - **OOM on big cell → `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, n_neighbors=10)`** — R-tree, same accuracy, less RAM. - **HT screen / very large system → `dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, coarse_factor=2)`** — 8× faster, mild smoothing. - **Python/Dask composition → `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000)`** — slowest, but lazy-friendly. - **NEVER → `dgrid_from_atoms_gpu`, `dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb`** — broken on skewed cells. ## Next steps - [Distance Grid tutorial](distance_grid.qmd) — basic usage, spacing tradeoffs, visualization. - [Benchmark: Rust AABB dgrid](benchmark_rust_aabb_dgrid.md) — performance numbers across methods. - [Region Segmentation](region_segmentation.qmd) — what happens after the distance grid. - [Appyling Periodic Boundary Conditions](applying_pbc.qmd) — PBC group structure on top of the segmentation. ## Related documentation - `mofography.rust_fun.dgrid_from_atoms_rust` - `mofography.rust_fun.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust` - `mofography.rust_fun.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust` - `mofography.compute.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu` (active, correct) - `mofography.compute.dgrid_from_atoms_gpu` (broken on skewed cells — do not use) - `mofography.compute.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb` (broken on skewed cells — do not use)
